opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think so, though maybe not for the reasons people expect. I don't think most people today will build a PCFG and deploy it. That era is mostly over. But PCFGs are one of the cleanest examples we have of a structured probabilistic model where you can actually do things exactly. You can compute the marginal likelihood, run inside-outside, get exact posteriors over trees, and see how dynamic programming and probability fit together. That way of thinking, what's tractable, what structure you're assuming, what you can compute versus what you have to approximate, carries over to a lot of modern problems.

A lot of what we see in large language models is a question of whether they're implicitly learning something like hierarchical structure. If you've never thought carefully about what a grammar is, or what it means for a model to represent constituency, it's hard to ask good questions about that. Some of the most interesting interpretability and formal-language work right now asks things like: can a transformer recognize this class of languages, and how does it simulate a stack or a parse? PCFGs give you the vocabulary for that.

There's also been a small revival in my own area. We've worked on compound PCFGs and neural parameterizations of grammars, and on scaling these models to large numbers of nonterminals with low-rank tricks. It turns out you can make these classical models much more expressive with neural networks while keeping the nice inference properties. I don't think they'll beat a giant transformer at language modeling. But as a scientific tool for understanding latent structure, they're still useful.

So I wouldn't tell a new student to spend a year on PCFGs. But spending a couple of weeks really understanding them, deriving inside-outside and implementing CKY, is worth it. It's like learning HMMs and the forward algorithm. You may never use them directly, but they shape how you think about sequence models for the rest of your career.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say yes, but maybe not for the reason people expect.

Nobody is going to beat a pretrained transformer on parsing accuracy with a PCFG at this point, so if the question is "should I build systems with them," the honest answer is probably no. But that was never really what they were for. The value of studying something like a PCFG is that it's a complete, understandable system. You can write down the model in a few lines, you know exactly what independence assumptions you're making, you can derive the inference algorithm by hand, and you can look at the output and know precisely why the model did what it did. That's a kind of clarity we've basically lost with large models, and I think it's a muscle you want to have built before you start working on systems where you can't see inside.

The second thing is that the machinery around them, dynamic programming over structures, inside-outside, marginalization over latent trees, doesn't go away. A lot of what's interesting right now in things like structured attention, latent variable models, or even thinking about what a transformer is implicitly computing, draws on exactly those ideas. When I taught this stuff, students who had actually implemented CKY and inside-outside understood things like the connection between semirings and backprop much faster than students who hadn't.

So I'd frame it this way: study them as a way to learn how to think about structure and inference, not as a tool you'll ship. The specific model is a bit of a museum piece. The way of thinking is still very much alive.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think it does, although I’d separate learning about them from deciding to use them in a system today. A probabilistic context-free grammar gives you a really concrete setting for thinking about latent structure. You observe a sentence, but you don’t observe the tree that generated it. So how do you sum over all those possible trees? How do you find the best one? How do you learn the parameters? Those are useful questions well beyond parsing.

And the algorithms are beautiful. You have this exponentially large space of structures, but you can compute things exactly by exploiting shared subproblems. Understanding why that works—and which assumptions make it possible—is valuable even when you move to models where exact inference isn’t practical.

So I wouldn’t say everyone doing NLP needs to spend months studying grammar formalisms. But implementing the inside algorithm, understanding the distinction between finding the most likely structure and marginalizing over structures—that’s a pretty good investment. The particular model might not be what you use next week, but the way of thinking carries over.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think so. I wouldn’t necessarily tell someone that the next system they build should use a probabilistic context-free grammar. But studying them gives you a really useful way to think about latent structure, dynamic programming, and the relationship between a model and the algorithms you use to do inference in it.

You have this compact mathematical object, and you can ask: How do I sum over all the possible trees? How do I find the best one? How do I learn when I don’t observe the structure? Those questions come up all over machine learning, even when the objects don’t look like grammars anymore.

So I’d distinguish learning about PCFGs from committing to them as the right model of language. You can be pretty skeptical of the latter and still get a lot out of the former.
